<reason>A establishes the stronger decision rule: assess total public value and credible access rather than make high unit prices an automatic veto. It directly answers double-payment, hospital-budget, and rationing objections while explaining why guaranteed demand need not make low-volume development viable at low prices. B raises legitimate budget and bargaining concerns, but repeatedly assumes equivalent cheaper supply and treats permission as surrendering negotiating leverage. Its demand for a verified developer walk-away does not defeat A’s permissible economic mechanism. A also exposes the tension between B’s prohibition and its willingness to revisit terms and pay more.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s pressure question forces B to concede that centrally purchasing expensive courses and supplying hospitals free remains an AMC. This defeats B’s subscription-based dismissal. A then distinguishes manufacturer price from patient access, leaving B needing to establish unnecessary expenditure rather than merely point to a high per-course price.</best_rebuttal>
